summary.text: A previously healthy 16-year-old female competitive dancer developed persistent right knee pain after a traumatic injury during a national dance competition, when she landed on her bent right knee while spinning. She kept performing the same move for 6 months. Orthopedic evaluation included an MRI showing a loculated fluid collection anterior to the tibial tubercle, and right knee aspiration gave only transient pain relief.

Five months later she saw her pediatrician for ongoing pain and was referred to rheumatology with a positive ANA of 1:320 (speckled). The initial rheumatologic exam was nondiagnostic, ANA stayed positive, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, anti-RNP and anti-SSA were negative, blood count, liver enzymes and thyroid function were normal, and a low vitamin D level of 28 ng/mL was addressed with supplementation.

At follow-up 10 months after the injury she had persistent pain below the right patella, which had become visibly indented, easy bruising and episodic swelling after dance. Exam showed a tender purplish gray atrophic plaque with prominent vessels and no mass; von Willebrand testing was negative and factor VIII mildly elevated. Ultrasound showed a fluid collection with skin as thin as 1.0 mm, not consistent with bursitis. Dermatology found a yellow-pink atrophic plaque and faint left knee ecchymosis.

Based on the clinical findings, imaging and absence of serologic evidence of autoimmune disease, she was diagnosed with a chronic Morel-Lavallée lesion, likely due to repetitive mechanical stress from competitive dancing. To date she has not pursued treatment.

article_limitations: Caption-layer visual status is not_inspected; the three JPEG figures are inspected in the separate visual target.
The MRI is "consistent with" a Morel-Lavallée lesion in the abstract but "suggestive of either" a hematoma or the lesion in the case text; the case-text wording is used.
The authors' shearing-force mechanism and delayed-healing statements are hypotheses ("likely", "potentially") and are recorded only as possible.
Discussion statements about pediatric Morel-Lavallée lesions in general are not patient facts.
No tables, supplements or videos are listed in the source.
"Five months later" orders the pediatrician visit after the adjacent aspiration sentence only; its interval reference point is not stated.
